papers.title: Macroscopic Nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer Mediated by Coherent Magnons
papers.abstract: Phonon-mediated nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer (RET) in metal deuterides is severely constrained by inertial rest-mass dilution, lattice fracture limits, and thermal nuclear spin cancellation. Extending the generalized nuclear Dicke model to Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR) magnons eliminates mass dilution via hyperfine-amplified M1 coupling while unlocking relativistic Dirac M2 coupling via Overhauser spin polarization. We derive a Suhl-clamped FMR scaling law predicting 14.2 MeV (Pd-106) and 11.4 MeV (Ni-58) breakup neutrons, 19.9 MeV alpha particles, and reconciled sub-keV fusion anomalies.

papers.title: A trap-based platform for cooling and laser spectroscopy of fast ions toward radioactive-ion applications
papers.abstract: We report on the first experiments with the Stopping and Trapping of Radioactive Isotopes for Precision Experiments (STRIPE) segmented linear Paul trap. The intent for this apparatus is to serve as an efficient capture and laser-cooling trap for radioactive isotopes produced at radioactive ion beam facilities. We demonstrate the deceleration of 10 keV ion beams and their trapping and laser cooling into Coulomb crystals. As an initial spectroscopic benchmark, the dipole-forbidden $5s$ $^2S_{1/2}$ $\rightarrow$ $4d$ $^2D_{5/2}$ transition in $^{88}$Sr$^+$ was driven, partially resolving the Zeeman structure and yielding a Gaussian linewidth of 14.5(8) MHz, with the residual width attributed to the ions' micromotion. The lifetime of the metastable $4d$ $^2D_{5/2}$ state was measured to be 0.325(5)$_{\mathrm{stat}}$(4)$_{\mathrm{sys}}$ s, uncorrected for collisional quenching. Several measurements to quantify the cooling timescale, the detection rate of the photon collection region and the trap storage lifetime were also performed. The developed technique will allow radioactive ion beams to be decelerated and cooled for precision spectroscopy measurements.

papers.title: 1.56 THz Full-Field Rydberg-Atom Imaging with 0.3 mm-scale Spatial Response
papers.abstract: THz imaging via Rydberg-atom up-conversion offers a powerful full-field modality with high sensitivity and rapid acquisition. However sub-millimeter imaging above 1 THz is still constrained by source power and beam-delivery loss. In this paper, we demonstrate a \(50~\mathrm{mm} \times 50~\mathrm{mm}\) full-field imaging at 1.56~THz by implementing the \(11P_{3/2} \rightarrow 10D_{5/2}\) transition of a cesium Rydberg-atom vapor. The measured spatial response FWHMs are \(0.314~\mathrm{mm}\) in horizontal and \(0.354~\mathrm{mm}\) in vertical for a \(0.5~\mathrm{mm}\) pinhole, alongside a sensitivity of \(31.7~\mathrm{fW}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}/(6.5 \times 6.5)~\mu\mathrm{m}^{2}\), and a frame rate up to \(300~\mathrm{fps}\). Under matched illumination, relay, and image-processing conditions, mask imaging at 1.56 THz reproduces finer features and edges with substantially higher edge contrast, deeper intensity-trough separation in line profiles, and recovered detail that remains blurred or unresolved at 0.55 THz. Furthermore, preliminary imaging of a \(200~\mu\mathrm{m}\) tissue slice suggests morphological correspondence with H\&E histology histology, offered as a proof-of-concept for label-free tissue characterization. By validating the wavelength-dependent resolution scaling in Rydberg THz imaging, this work establishes frequency scaling as a general design principle for sub-millimeter Rydberg-THz imaging.

papers.title: Quantum phase estimation on a Rydberg quantum simulator
papers.abstract: Determining the energy spectrum of a many-body quantum system is a central goal of quantum physics. Ground-state energies underpin materials science and quantum chemistry, whereas excited states govern dynamical phenomena such as quantum thermalization. Quantum simulators have greatly shaped our understanding of many-body systems, for example, by enabling access to microscopic mechanisms and nonlocal order parameters. However, experiments still struggle to access the full range of many-body spectral features and are typically limited to measuring energy gaps and excitations by spectroscopic means. Here, we address this challenge by demonstrating quantum phase estimation on an analog Rydberg quantum simulator. We reconstruct the complex-valued return amplitude, or Loschmidt echo, of an initial probe state. From its Fourier transform, we measure absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in systems of up to 19 atoms in one and two spatial dimensions. Varying the initial probe state, we select distinct spectral windows within which we compute the longitudinal and transverse magnetization, and observe their competition across the many-body spectrum. Our results thereby demonstrate phase-sensitive many-body spectroscopy on an analog quantum simulator without auxiliary qubits or controlled evolution.
